bot-defeat.title: The bot-defeat saga
bot-defeat.subtitle: Getting real supplier data without a browser farm — and knowing, with evidence, when you can't.
bot-defeat.body:
Travel supplier portals sit behind some of the most aggressive anti-bot stacks on the public internet — Akamai Bot Manager Premier, DataDome, TLS fingerprinting. The industry default is a Playwright browser farm on VMs. Voygent's discipline is the opposite: probe first, and only pay for a browser where the evidence says you must.

The probe ladder

Every supplier goes through the same escalation: curl-impersonate locally → a disposable Cloudflare Worker probing from CF egress → Playwright last. Each probe leaves a falsifiable artifact (docs/probes/*.md plus a runnable probe Worker), so a verdict is never a vibe — it can be re-run and overturned.

And verdicts do get overturned, in both directions:

  • A 2026-04-29 re-probe flipped three excursion providers (Tours by Locals, Shore Excursions Group, GetYourGuide) from "browser-required, abandoned" to worker-viable with no credentials — the old verdicts predated the curl-impersonate discipline.
  • CPMaxx — long framed as browser-gated — turned out to be plain nginx from a Worker. The whole CPMaxx suite (hotels, cruise, air, cars, tours, transfers) now runs as native Worker fetch() adapters, with the old browser path demoted to fallback. The misclassification itself is documented and corrected in the repo's history.
  • The reverse, too: AA Vacations looked worker-viable from a warm browser, but a byte-certified CF-egress probe showed the login POST 403s while the GET passes — the "worker-viable" read was falsified and recorded as such.

The Carnival forensics

The deepest investigation characterized a modern Akamai BMP deployment end-to-end. Eight Playwright configurations, two residential proxy vendors, byte-level diffing of 491,810 sensor reads — byte-identical across an AT&T Mobility and a Comcast residential path. Conclusion: the gate isn't the JS sensor surface at all; it's connection-layer (L4) proxy-indirection detection. No amount of browser-fingerprint work fixes that, and a Workers fetch() trips the same gate.

That result is codified as an architecture decision (voygent-lite docs/adr/0003) with explicit re-open triggers — so nobody burns a week re-testing Carnival-class suppliers without new evidence. Knowing where the wall is, with receipts, is as valuable as the wins.

The catalog today: ~23 suppliers classified, ~30 adapters running on Workers fetch() — TLS/JA3-sensitive integrations from a serverless edge runtime, where the industry default is a VM farm.

context-economics.title: Context economics
context-economics.subtitle: An agent's real budget isn't dollars — it's the model's context window. Voygent engineers that budget deliberately.
context-economics.body:
Every tool schema, every raw search payload, every rendered document the model sees costs context — and context costs latency, money, and reasoning quality. Voygent treats the context window as a metered resource with explicit engineering around what enters it.

Router consolidation: ~70 tools → ~35

Per-supplier tools don't scale: ChatGPT caps connectors around 35 tools, and every schema rides in every request. The fix is per-domain router tools — cruise_search(line), flight_search(source), hotel_search(source) — with the supplier as an argument. Fewer names, smaller catalog, same coverage; downstream adapters keep stable name + inputSchema contracts so the router calls them unchanged.

This lands as a risk-sequenced migration, not a big-bang rename — and the sequencing is the point. A cruise pilot shipped first (cruise_search + cruise_detail replacing ~18 standalones — −17 catalog names, live in production), proving the router-over-adapter pattern before it scaled. A five-domain fan-out follows (flight / hotel / package / car / excursion). Crucially, the old per-supplier tools are retired only after their router is verified equivalent against the live adapters — the deletion is gated on a passing parity check, never on faith. You can watch the count fall as each wave lands: the "MCP tools exposed" stat in this demo's Engineering panel is the size of that catalog.

Search → distill → stage by id

Raw supplier responses are huge (a single flight search can be hundreds of KB). They never enter the model. Searches write to a server-side candidate store; the model reads a distilled list (flight_list) and stages a pick by candidate id — the server joins the id back to the full data. The model carries a pointer, not the payload. This demo's Engineering tab shows the per-call savings live.

Documents render out-of-context

The client-facing trip document (the "folio") is a deterministic template render on the server — the model never generates or even sees the HTML. A document the model would have burned tens of thousands of output tokens writing (badly, with hallucination risk) is produced from structured trip state for zero model tokens. The model patches structured fields; the renderer does the rest.

Patches, not rewrites

Trip state mutates through patch_trip — field-level updates against server-held state — rather than round-tripping the whole trip JSON through the model each turn. The demo's "context kept out of the model" panel is measuring exactly this.

Schemas are context too

Consolidation shrinks the number of tools; the next lever is the weight of each schema. A measured proposal (voygent-lite ADR-0007, characterized on a schema-eval harness — not yet in src) replaces a literal source enum with a smaller semantic discriminator — the model says what it needs, and a server-side INTENT_MAP resolves that to the supplier. Across five models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and two OpenAI models) it held ~90% dispatch accuracy while cutting per-tool schema tokens ~54%. Fewer tools and leaner schemas per tool — the two compound. It's filed as a proposal precisely because the demo's honesty rule is to call shipped "shipped" and a finding "a finding."

record-replay.title: Record/replay engineering
record-replay.subtitle: How a public demo shows real data deterministically — with fabrication made structurally impossible.
record-replay.body:
A public LLM demo has a credibility problem: if the model can write travel data into the page, it will eventually invent a flight. This demo's first build did exactly that — the folio looked perfect and was hallucinated. The fix wasn't a sterner prompt. It was structural.

Capture once, replay byte-for-byte

For the five featured trips, a capture script runs the real production pipeline once — real searches, real candidate lists, and crucially the real promoted trip objects keyed by candidate id. The demo's replay layer intercepts the search tools and serves those captures. When the model picks a hotel, the server writes the captured object for that candidate id — the model authors only the id, never the data. An id with no fixture match is rejected. There is no code path by which model-invented data reaches the folio.

Live trips are the opposite — faithfully

Ask for a destination outside the featured five and the session latches into live mode: every tool call passes through to the production Voygent MCP, the full tool catalog is exposed, and the folio renders exactly what read_trip returns. Featured trips are the rehearsed "gif"; live trips are the real product, unsanitized.

The harness tests itself the same way

The same recording format drives the autoplay demo, and a headless smoke harness drives the full SSE pipeline — scripted board picks, sequencing assertions ("no hotel board before a flight is picked"), and an enrichment verdict — against local or production. Sessions survive Durable Object eviction by persisting conversation + replay state, so an idle reader doesn't orphan their trip.

Demo honesty is an engineering property, not a policy: the rejected-id test and the client-data allowlist are unit-tested invariants.

cost-engineering.title: Cost engineering
cost-engineering.subtitle: What an agent session actually costs, why caching changes the math, and why MCP's economics favor the product.
cost-engineering.body:
This demo runs a full agent loop — Anthropic Messages API, streaming, the production tool catalog — on a public URL. That only works if cost is engineered, not hoped about.

Prompt caching does the heavy lifting

An agent loop re-sends its whole history every turn. Uncached, that re-bills the full conversation as fresh input each time. The demo places cache breakpoints on the three expensive prefixes — the tool catalog, the long static seed prompt, and a moving breakpoint on the final message so the whole growing conversation is a cache hit next turn. Cache reads bill at ~0.1× fresh input; writes at ~1.25×. The Engineering tab reports the session's cache hit rate and a cost-weighted token figure (reads at 0.1×, writes at 1.25×) — the honest number to compare against a subscription window, where the raw sum would read 5–10× too pessimistic.

Defense in depth on a public endpoint

  • Per-conversation caps (turns + tool calls), enforced server-side.
  • A global daily spend ledger in a reserved Durable Object — the endpoint pauses itself at the cap.
  • An instant kill switch (DEMO_DISABLED secret — no redeploy).
  • A destructive-tool denylist: the public catalog withholds deletes, client-facing publishes, and CRM writes.

The MCP business case

The structural point: under the MCP model, the product's marginal inference cost is $0 — the user's own Claude subscription pays for the tokens, and these sessions fit comfortably inside a plan's 5-hour window (the demo's plan table computes your session's exact share, cost-weighted). A standalone app must meter API tokens, mark them up, and carry billing/abuse/infra liability that compounds with volume and model tier. An MCP product ships frontier-model reasoning at flat rate, and its costs don't scale with its users' usage.

production-system.title: The system behind the demo
production-system.subtitle: This demo fronts a production MCP product. These are capabilities of that system — the demo's live panel shows only what your session actually did.
production-system.body:
Scale, on the edge

119 tool registrations, ~30 supplier adapters across cruise / flight / hotel / package / car / excursion — all on Cloudflare Workers fetch(), no browser and no VM for anything that probes worker-viable. One MCP server drives both Claude and ChatGPT (OAuth 2.1 + Dynamic Client Registration, per-user URL+token auth, a tier-gated catalog locked per session).

The commission firewall

Advisors earn commission; clients must never see it. That separation is a codified law, not a convention: the client render path runs an explicit field allowlist plus assertNoAdvisorKeys, and economics are served separately behind bearer auth with no-store. The invariant has a grep-verify and lives in a six-law LAWS.md enforced by a read-only "curator" verification agent whose cardinal rule is no evidence → no verdict. (This demo's advisor toggle is the inverse, deliberately: demo boards are the advisor view, so commission is a feature.)

AI evaluates the AI

A persona/judge evaluation harness exercises the real product: 13 advisor personas × 22 scenarios make live MCP calls, and a higher-grade judge model scores each run on four weighted dimensions — task completion, UX, data quality, error handling. Regressions auto-file issues with generated fix prompts. Eval-driven development in production, not in a notebook.

Vendor onboarding as a pipeline

Adding a supplier is one command: probe (the ladder from the bot-defeat saga) → classify → scaffold from a category-matched template → wire into the router and tier catalog → generate tests → staged commit. An audit mode re-runs a shipped adapter against captured baselines and files an issue when it drifts.

Telemetry that can't hurt the hot path

One non-blocking Analytics Engine data point per tool call at the tier-gate chokepoint — no-ops when the binding is absent, and unit-tested to never throw even if the telemetry write itself throws. Fire-and-forget by construction.

Credentials it never sees in the clear

Advisors bring their own supplier logins. Each secret is stored per-user in D1 under envelope encryption — a per-user AES-256-GCM key wraps every value — and the vault tool returns only presence and metadata, never a stored value, even back to the advisor who set it. Every set, delete, and test writes an audit row, the scope is locked to travel-supplier portals, and a vendor's tools stay out of your catalog until its credentials exist. (ADR-0010.)

Nothing ships unverified

Production has a gate. A prod deploy is refused unless a same-SHA staging smoke test passed within the hour and a 7-boundary security suite is green — cross-tenant isolation, the auth front door, call-time tier enforcement, the app-only data channel, render XSS, SSRF, and proxy/secret hygiene. Writing those tests turned up and fixed two live vulnerability classes. Between deploys, a nightly QA digest and a token-gated ops dashboard watch the system.

How this demo is built

The reel you just watched replays a real planning session through the same reducer the live app uses, so it is pixel-identical to a live run and costs $0 to play — and it cannot fabricate data, because replay returns fixtures and the authoring DSL rejects any pick that is not a real candidate id. The annotated callouts are made with cueframe, a tool built for this: give it a URL and a plain-English workflow, it drives the page with Playwright and anchors each callout to a real DOM element instead of a fixed pixel, so the annotations survive a re-record when the UI moves.

data-stores.title: KV, D1, and rewiring a SQL brain
data-stores.subtitle: Four storage primitives, one hybrid model, and the unlearning a career relational DBA has to do at the edge.
data-stores.body:
Voygent runs on Cloudflare's edge, where "the database" is really four primitives with sharply different shapes. The discipline is to match each piece of state to the primitive whose grain fits it, and to resist the old habit of forcing everything into rows and joins.

The four primitives

  • Workers KV: a global, eventually-consistent key/value store. O(1) get/put by key, list by key prefix. No queries, no joins, roughly 60s global propagation. Voygent keeps each trip blob here under a caller-prefixed key.
  • D1: SQLite at the edge, with real SQL, transactions, indexes, and FTS5 full-text search. Voygent uses it as the catalog and index, the queryable spine (find trips, search content) that KV can't express.
  • R2: object storage for binaries such as rendered folio HTML, images, and documents. Served by path, billed like S3, with no egress fees.
  • Durable Objects: a single-writer, strongly-consistent compute and storage cell, running serialized transactions against one logical owner. This demo's per-session state (conversation, replay snapshot, the daily-budget ledger) lives in a DO, exactly the workload KV's eventual consistency can't safely hold.

The hybrid model

A trip is written as a KV blob (cheap, global, read-heavy) and also indexed as a D1 row, so listing an advisor's trips or searching trip content stays a single indexed query. R2 holds what the client downloads. DO holds the live, must-be-consistent session. Each store does the one job it's shaped for.

The mindshift for a career SQL DBA

If your instinct is "third-normal-form, then JOIN," the edge will fight you. The rewiring:

  • Key design is the schema. In KV there's no WHERE, only the key and its prefix. You design the key so the access you need is a get or a list, because nothing else exists.
  • No cross-key joins. You denormalize on purpose, duplicating the fields a read needs straight into the blob so the read never has to join. Storage is cheap; an extra round trip at the edge is expensive.
  • Eventual consistency is the default. A KV write may take up to a minute to become globally visible, so treat that as expected behaviour. Anything that needs read-your-writes (a counter, a lock, a ledger) belongs in a DO or D1.
  • A list is an ordered prefix scan. Results come back paginated and sorted by key, so you encode sort order and grouping into the key itself: zero-padded indices and sortable timestamps, like padding message keys as msg:00000 so a list returns them in order.
  • Reach for D1 when you genuinely need a query. Full-text search, ad-hoc filters, and aggregates are what D1's FTS5 and SQL are for. The skill is knowing which reads justify the index and which are just a keyed blob fetch.
  • Values have hard caps. A DO storage value caps at 128 KiB, and a real tool-result bundle can exceed it, so the persisted copy elides its largest payloads to fit while the in-memory copy stays whole. The cap is a constraint you plan around.
The relational reflexes still have a place; they are just scoped now. You keep SQL where SQL earns its keep, in D1, and you stop paying join cost for reads that a well-designed key answers for free.

llm-options.title: Choosing the model — and why the demo is LLM-agnostic
llm-options.subtitle: Frontier, cheap, and local models behind one provider seam. The moat is the tools and the orchestration, not the model vendor.
llm-options.body:
This demo drives a full agent loop, but the model behind it is swappable. Everything the agent does — the tool catalog, the trip state, the record/replay honesty layer — sits behind a single provider interface, so the driving LLM is a configuration choice, not a rewrite.

The seam

One TypeScript interface, LLMProvider.stream(messages, tools, opts), yields a normalized event stream (text deltas, tool calls, token usage). Anthropic's Claude is one implementation; a DeepSeekProvider over the OpenAI-compatible API is another; an OllamaProvider for local models is a third. The agent loop consumes the normalized events and never knows which vendor produced them. Adding a provider is implementing one interface plus a pricing row.

Frontier vs cheap vs local

  • Frontier (Anthropic Claude). Strongest reasoning and tool-use reliability; the default for the demo's discovery phase. Anthropic-specific prompt-cache breakpoints make a long agent loop affordable — cache reads bill at ~0.1× fresh input.
  • Cheap (DeepSeek). An OpenAI-compatible, very-low-cost model — the same family this project's own bulk-I/O tooling routes to. It does automatic prefix caching (no manual breakpoints) and reports cache hits directly. Great for the recipe-driven enrichment phase where the reasoning bar is lower. The "optimize for cost" preset routes here.
  • Local (Ollama). A model on your own machine — zero per-token cost, full data residency, offline-capable. In this demo it is shown but grayed out: this UI is served from a Cloudflare edge Worker, which cannot reach a model listening on your localhost. The provider exists in code; it only lights up in a local-dev deployment where OLLAMA_BASE_URL is reachable.

Speed vs cost vs capability

The Tweaks panel exposes three presets. Speed favors the fastest small model; Cost routes to the cheapest enabled provider; Capability puts the strongest model on the reasoning-heavy phase. "Smart" routing can even split phases across vendors — frontier discovery, cheap enrichment — because the seam makes per-turn provider choice free.

Honesty survives the swap

For the featured trips, the replay layer intercepts tool results, not the model — so swapping providers can't let any model fabricate travel data. A weaker model that picks a nonexistent option id simply gets rejected. The model-agnostic seam and the fabrication guard are orthogonal, by design.

When local actually wins

Grayed here doesn't mean useless. Local models win when data must never leave the building (regulated/PII workloads), when token cost at scale dominates (high-volume batch classification), or when the deployment must run offline. The right architecture is the one that lets you make that call per-workload — which is exactly what the provider seam buys.

phase-machine.title: Keeping the model on track
phase-machine.subtitle: A server-side phase machine drives the build and hands the model one small instruction at a time — which is exactly what lets a cheaper model do the job reliably.
phase-machine.body:
An open-ended agent loop asks a lot of the model: hold the whole multi-step plan in its head, decide what's next, and never drift. A frontier model mostly manages it. A cheaper, smaller model mostly doesn't — it stops early (declares a trip "done" before enrichment), presents instead of acting (asks "shall I add restaurants?" instead of calling the tool), or narrates from memory (names a plausible-sounding restaurant no tool ever returned). Those aren't reasoning failures — the small model is smart enough for each step. They're discipline failures across a long sequence.

Move the sequencing into the server

The phase machine takes the trip build off the model's shoulders. A pure, unit-tested reducer (worker/agent/phases.ts) owns a small state machine — INTAKE → FLIGHT_PICK → HOTEL_SEARCH → HOTEL_PICK → ENRICH_EXCURSIONS → APPLY_PICKS → ENRICH_DINING → SUMMARY — and the worker, not the model, decides what happens next. Before each turn the model is handed one small directive: the current phase's instruction, and nothing else.

Advance by observation, never by trust

The machine only moves forward when it observes the right tool actually succeed. advancePhase(phase, toolName, input, result) watches the real tool-result stream: a successful flight_search moves INTAKE → FLIGHT_PICK; a successful promote_hotels_to_lodging moves HOTEL_PICK → ENRICH_EXCURSIONS. A failed or unrelated call doesn't advance. The model can't talk its way forward — it has to do the thing.

If it stops mid-build, re-prompt it

When the model ends its turn without a tool call — the classic "I'll stop here" — a capped auto-continuation re-issues the current phase's directive and keeps going. The build can't quietly wedge half-finished. And there's an escape hatch: after a few re-prompts the machine forces the SUMMARY step, so a trip always gets a clean closing message rather than trailing off. (In the board-pick phases it does the opposite on purpose: a stop there is the model correctly waiting for you, so it doesn't auto-continue.)

Why this is the cheap-model unlock

Reliability now comes from the structure, not from the model's stamina — so you can run the whole build on a much cheaper model. The acceptance bar for this work: with Claude Haiku driving, 10 out of 10 scripted Dublin builds produced a complete folio — 3+ day-by-day days, at least one free and one paid activity, 4+ dining picks, and zero fabricated names. Before the phase machine, Haiku routinely stalled before enrichment. Same model; the difference is who holds the plan.

It pairs with model routing

That dovetails with the model-agnostic provider seam: once the structure carries correctness, you can route the reasoning-light phases to the cheapest capable model and reserve a stronger model only for the parts that need it — or run the entire build on the cheap model and let the harness keep it honest. The phase machine is what makes "offload to a cheaper model" a safe default instead of a gamble.

Shipped the careful way

The whole machine is gated behind a single environment flag (DEMO_PHASE_MACHINE). Flag off, the behavior is byte-identical to the previous open-loop path; flag on, the worker drives. It shipped dormant, was canaried on production, and rolls back instantly by deleting one secret — no redeploy. You can watch it step live in this demo's Engineering panel: the "Workflow engine" trail shows each phase the server advanced through as your trip is built.

The general lesson for agent products: don't ask a cheap model to be disciplined for twenty turns — make the discipline a property of the system, and let the model do the one small thing in front of it. The same orchestration discipline is what would let the production MCP make cheaper host models viable, too.

trip-integrity.title: Trip integrity: the data is the product
trip-integrity.subtitle: A weak model will ship a blank or fabricated proposal unless the server won't let it. Voygent owns data quality end-to-end.
trip-integrity.body:
The validation panel in this demo's Engineering tab — the "validation N/N" stat and the Trip integrity ✓ / ↻ / ✗ checks — isn't cosmetic. It's the visible edge of a production stance: the trip data is the deliverable, so its correctness is enforced by the server, not hoped for from the model. This is a different concern from record/replay (that's about the public demo never showing invented data); this is about the live product refusing to emit a bad proposal in the first place.

Lite owns it end-to-end

An earlier architecture split the work — one service wrote raw trip JSON, another "reconciled" it later. Voygent collapsed that: data-quality findings (duplicate booking shapes, a missing amount, a double-encoded HTML entity, a price that doesn't sum) are bugs fixed at the source, on write, in one place. The decision is codified (voygent-lite ADR-0006) so the ownership can't quietly drift back apart.

Guard, don't hope

The strongest guards are the ones a model literally cannot talk past. preview_folio_board carries an empty-decisions guard — it will not render a client proposal with no choices in it, which is exactly the failure mode a rushed or cheap model produces. A decisions builder assembles pickable options from trip state, and a completenessHint rides back in tool metadata to nudge the model toward the gaps. On the write path, validateAndCleanTripData normalizes shapes and reconcilePricing makes the numbers add up before anything is shown to a client.

Advisory vs. blocking — on purpose

Not every warning should stop the world. patch_trip returns consistencyWarnings[] — amber, non-blocking signals ("this hotel's dates don't overlap the trip", "this leg has no price") that surface to the advisor without halting the build. The hard guards block a publish; the advisories inform a human. The split is deliberate: over-blocking trains people to bypass the guard.

Self-heal — the "↻ repaired" checks

Some problems are better fixed than flagged. When a published proposal URL once resolved to /proposal/unknown (a missing trip id), the fix wasn't a louder error — the builder now stamps meta.tripId at save time and the render path self-heals the link. Duplicate-booking shapes get normalized; double-encoded entities get decoded. Those are the runs that show as ↻ repaired in the panel above: the server caught a flaw and corrected it, rather than passing it to a client.

Demo honesty (replay) and product integrity (these guards) are two different invariants, both structural. One stops the demo from lying; the other stops the product from shipping a blank or broken proposal — even when a cheap model is driving.

subagents.title: Subagents for the drudge work
subagents.subtitle: Routine inbox-and-offers toil, handled by an agent that proposes and never disposes — the advisor stays in the loop by construction.
subagents.body:
A travel advisor's day is full of necessary tedium: triaging a flooded inbox, pulling promo codes out of supplier blasts, matching a booking confirmation to the right active trip. It's exactly the work an agent should absorb — and exactly the work where a wrong autonomous action (a deleted email, a message sent to the wrong client) does real damage. Voygent's answer is a subagent that does the reading and the drafting but holds no authority to act. It proposes; the human disposes.

The shipped one: the offers inbox

This isn't hypothetical — it runs today against a real advisor mailbox. An IMAP IDLE watcher (a systemd service) reacts to mail as it arrives. A Haiku-4.5 classifier sorts each message into one of 13 categories (promo blast, booking confirmation, client-active, supplier doc, junk…), and anything it isn't sure about — confidence under 0.6 — is parked as UNCERTAIN rather than guessed. A second pass pulls structured offers (code, type, dates) out of the promo blasts and posts them straight into Voygent's shared offers index, where they become searchable inventory for trip-building. A trip-linker matches operational mail to the advisor's live trips. Every morning a deterministic 06:00 digest — pure SQL→markdown, zero LLM calls, so it can't hallucinate — lands as the advisor's triage queue. To date: ~3,700 messages ingested, ~2,300 classified, for about $4.50 of model spend.

Propose, never dispose

The safety model is structural, not a promise. The watcher opens the mailbox read-only — IMAP EXAMINE, never SELECT for write — so a code path that calls STORE, MOVE, EXPUNGE, or APPEND is treated as a bug, not a feature. DRY_RUN is the default and the only permitted value in this phase: actions the agent recommends are written to an actions table with executed_at left NULL — a log of proposed moves, nothing performed. The advisor works the digest (or a mobile triage view) and decides. The codified rule, in priority order: mailbox safety > classification correctness > feature completeness > speed. When two goals collide, the human's data wins.

Coming soon — the rest of the fleet

The offers agent is the first of a pattern, and the pattern generalizes to other advisor drudge work — each piece coming soon, each built the same propose-don't-dispose way:

  • Offers into the trip. Today the agent files offers into the index; next it surfaces the relevant ones inside the build — "three of your suppliers are running Greece promos this week" — as suggestions the advisor accepts, never auto-applied.
  • An adapter-audit watchdog. The same onboarding pipeline that ships a supplier adapter has an --audit mode that re-runs it against captured baselines. Run on a schedule as a subagent, it files an issue when a supplier site drifts — catching a broken integration before an advisor hits it live.
  • A trip-integrity sweeper. A background pass over trips that flags the data-quality issues the live guards would catch — stale prices, dangling bookings — and proposes the fix for review.
The principle that makes this safe to ship is the same one behind the phase machine: don't ask the model for judgment it shouldn't hold. An agent can read a thousand emails and draft every action — and still touch nothing until a human says go. Keeping the advisor in the loop isn't a limitation bolted on; it's the architecture.

context-economics-v2.title: Context economics
context-economics-v2.subtitle: Everything the model sees costs context. These are the levers I use to keep what enters the window small.
context-economics-v2.body:
Everything the model sees costs context: every tool schema, every raw search payload, every rendered document. Context costs latency, money, and reasoning quality, so I treat the window as a metered resource and engineer what gets to enter it. These are the levers, roughly in the order they started to hurt.

Too many tools

Voygent grew the way most complex systems built from scratch do: one tool at a time. I'd find a capability the assistant was missing, build that single tool, wire it into the MCP, and move on to the next gap. As my process for spotting what was needed got sharper, especially for travel-provider searches, I was adding several tools a week. That worked right up until the catalog grew out of control. It got too large for ChatGPT to load at all, and past a certain size it started to confuse even Claude Opus, which would reach for the wrong tool or stall choosing between near-duplicates.

The obvious way to expose 30 suppliers is one tool per supplier. That gave me roughly 70 tools. Two problems showed up fast. ChatGPT caps connectors at around 35 tools, so the catalog didn't even fit. And every tool schema rides along in every request, so a 70-tool catalog was paying context tax on all 70 schemas to make a single hotel search.

Getting to a working catalog at all took a lot of throwaway versions. One thing AI-assisted coding changed about how I work is what happens when a repo starts collapsing under the weight of its own patches and work-arounds. It's cheap to start over well. I can point Claude Code or Codex at the failing version, have it pull out the concepts and techniques that actually worked, write down the lessons learned from that attempt, and stand up a fresh repo that brings in only the parts worth keeping. I've been working on this AI travel assistant since October 2024 and I've lost count of the abandoned versions, but it's more than fifteen. Each one carried something forward into the next.

Once I finally had all the tools working, the next problem was consolidating them and refactoring everything that referred to them: call sites, prompts, and tool descriptions. This is the other place AI-assisted coding earns its keep. Subagents are good at methodically refactoring a whole codebase in a few hours, which is how I cut the tool count, shortened the descriptions, and trimmed the extra text the tools were returning into the model's context. I didn't want to guess at what to cut, so I built a test harness that A/B tests changes across several AI providers and models. That way the calls about which tools to merge, and how much of each result to send back, are backed by measurements instead of intuition.

TODO(neil): drop in the concrete savings figures from the harness run against the stripped-down Voygent MCP tools (per-provider/per-model token deltas, accuracy held). One or two representative numbers here makes the "evidence-based" claim land.

What I run now is one router tool per domain, with the supplier passed as an argument: cruise_search(line), flight_search(source), hotel_search(source). Fewer names in the catalog, smaller per-request payload, same supplier coverage. The adapters underneath keep their existing name and inputSchema, so the router calls them unchanged.

I didn't do this as a big-bang rename, because a rename that breaks live tool contracts is hard to walk back. I sequenced it by risk. The cruise pilot shipped first (cruise_search + cruise_detail replacing about 18 standalone tools, a net 17 names off the catalog, live in production), which proved the router-over-adapter pattern before I scaled it. A five-domain fan-out (flight, hotel, package, car, excursion) follows the same path. The old per-supplier tools only get deleted after their router passes a parity check against the live adapters. You can watch the catalog shrink as each wave lands: the "MCP tools exposed" number in this demo's Engineering panel is the size of that catalog.

The search results were the bigger cost

A single flight search comes back as hundreds of KB of supplier JSON. The naive path is to hand that to the model and let it pick. I tried that early on and it doesn't hold up: one search can blow the whole context budget, and the model still has to reason over raw vendor fields it doesn't really understand. What I do instead is write the full results to a server-side candidate store and hand the model a distilled list (flight_list) of a dozen or so options. The model stages a pick by candidate id, and the server joins that id back to the full record. The model holds the id and a short summary; the full payload stays server-side. The per-call savings show up live in this demo's Engineering panel.

The client document renders from state

This part took a winding path. My early trip-planning attempts were prompting only, and they made two gaps obvious. I needed a precise, persistent record of the plan that I could retrieve and edit, which is its own story about giving up the relational-database habit for a hybrid KV + D1 model. And I needed a consistent, presentable way to put a proposal in front of a client.

For the client-facing document I worked through a few formats. I tried rendered markdown, then PDF, and settled on HTML. The harder question was who writes the HTML. Asking Claude to produce the full itinerary and supporting detail as markup exploded the context and was prohibitively expensive, and since the documents were large, each change meant regenerating the whole thing rather than diffing it reliably. What worked was a template plus a Handlebars utility: structured trip data goes in, a complete and good-looking document comes out fast, and the model never touches the markup. I later moved to the HTML folio it is now, a plain web page that also happens to print to a clean format.

So the trip document the client sees, the folio, is one thing I deliberately keep the model away from. Having it generate the HTML would be tens of thousands of output tokens per render, it would be slow, and it would hallucinate both markup and numbers. So the model never writes it. The folio renders from structured trip state through a deterministic template on the server, for zero model tokens. The model patches fields; the renderer produces the page.

Trip edits go through patches

Trip state changes through patch_trip, which applies a field-level update to server-held state. The alternative, round-tripping the whole trip JSON through the model every turn, wastes tokens and invites drift as the model re-serializes a large object it only partly changed. The demo's "context kept out of the model" panel measures exactly this.

What's next: the schemas themselves

Consolidation cut the number of tools. The schemas that remain are the next lever, because every one of them still rides along in every request. I have a measured proposal (voygent-lite ADR-0007) that replaces a literal source enum with a smaller semantic discriminator: the model says what it needs, and a server-side INTENT_MAP resolves that to a supplier. On a schema-eval harness across five models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and two OpenAI models) it held about 90% dispatch accuracy while cutting per-tool schema tokens by ~54%. It is a finding, not shipped code, and I'm keeping it labeled that way until it lands in src.

bot-defeat-v2.title: The bot-defeat saga
bot-defeat-v2.subtitle: Getting real supplier data from a Cloudflare Worker, and knowing, with evidence, when you can't.
bot-defeat-v2.body:
Travel supplier portals sit behind some of the most aggressive anti-bot stacks on the public internet: Akamai Bot Manager Premier, DataDome, TLS fingerprinting. The industry default for getting data out of them is a Playwright browser farm on VMs. Voygent runs about 30 supplier adapters as plain Cloudflare Worker fetch() calls, no browser and no VM. This page is the story of how each supplier got classified, and I want to start with the part where I was wrong, because that record is what makes the rest of the verdicts worth trusting.

The verdict I had to take back

For a long time I had CPMaxx framed as a Carnival-class strict-BMP site that could not run from a Worker, and the architecture said so: the whole CPMaxx suite routed through a real browser, with the Worker as a client. Then on 2026-05-29 I probed it directly from the edge. A plain curl GET against /main/login came back 200 with the real login form, Server: nginx, no cf-ray, no _abck or bm_sz cookies, no challenge, no captcha, no CSRF token, no sensor script. CPMaxx is plain nginx from the edge. Its only browser-shaped requirement is the adzuki form-component submit protocol and holding a PHPSESSID, which is session plumbing, not bot defense. The misclassification is documented and corrected in the repo history (commit 846f1a8), and the CPMaxx suite (hotels, cruise, air, cars, tours, transfers) now runs as native Worker adapters with the old browser path demoted to fallback.

It cuts the other way too. AA Vacations looked worker-viable from a warm browser session and I recorded it as such. Byte-certified probing from Cloudflare egress later showed the login POST 403s even though the GET passes, so my own earlier verdict was falsified and the row flipped to browser-locked (docs/probes/2026-06-05-browser-locked-reexamination.md). FareBuzz went the same way. This is why every probe leaves a runnable artifact: a verdict is a claim with evidence attached, and it gets overturned in whichever direction the evidence points.

The challenge

The catalog behind all this is 23 supplier feasibility writeups, synthesized in docs/probes/2026-04-29-defense-bypass-catalog.md. The score so far: 8 shipped adapters (Carnival, MSC, Virgin Voyages, Expedia TAAP, GMT Cruiselink, Southwest via Playwright, CruisingPower desktop-only, SerpAPI), 9 provisional or waiting on credentials, 15 abandoned. The probe and build work came to roughly 21 to 27 days. Built suppliers averaged about two days each; abandoned ones cost about half a day, because they failed fast at the first gate. Failing cheap is the design.

The probe ladder

Every supplier goes through the same escalation: curl-impersonate locally, then a disposable Cloudflare Worker probing from CF egress, then Playwright last. The most valuable technique the ladder surfaced is also the cheapest one: fetch the supplier's home page first to seed the Akamai BMP cookies. That single move got 8 of the 13 reachable suppliers past their gate, and it costs one extra GET.

Five Akamai postures, five different answers

Akamai BMP turned out to deploy in five distinct postures, and what works against one does nothing against another.

Some portals have no BMP at the entry point at all (Virgin Voyages, Carnival's goccl.com agent portal). Nothing to clear. The most common posture is pass-through, where the _abck cookie arrives as ~-1~-1~-1~-1~-1 (Carnival consumer, MSC, Expedia TAAP, Princess, HAL, Regent, Disney): a GET first is enough, and workerd's TLS is accepted. I cleared this posture everywhere it appeared.

The other three postures are walls, each with a specific reason I stopped pushing. The bare 403 (AA Vacations, FareBuzz) is an IP/ASN/TLS denylist that fires before BMP even runs; residential curl gets the same 403, so there is nothing for a Worker to imitate. The workerd-specific TLS gate (Apple Vacations / VAX) passes curl and Node but fails identical headers sent from a Worker; workerd's rustls JA3 cannot be changed from inside a Worker, so the block is structural. The write-gate (Delta Vacations, Oceania, NCL) returns 200 on GET and 403 or 444 on POST, because _abck only flips to ~0~ after the sensor JavaScript runs against a real DOM, and a Worker has no DOM to offer. And when regimes stack (AA Vacations runs Akamai plus Cloudflare bot management), the bypass cost compounds rather than adds. All of these are abandoned, on the record, with the failing probe attached.

The bypasses that earned their writeups

MSC runs Next.js Server Actions whose action IDs rotate on every deploy build, so anything hardcoded breaks on the next MSC release. The adapter discovers the IDs at runtime instead: scrape the chunks, score the candidates, trial-label them, cache the result in KV. It self-heals on auth failure; a cache miss costs about 20 seconds of rediscovery, and then it is free until MSC ships again.

ToursByLocals, Shore Excursions Group, and GetYourGuide had all been written off as browser-required. Re-probed on 2026-04-29 with a real-Chrome JA3 from Worker egress, all three passed cleanly. They sit behind Cloudflare bot-management JA3 gates that Worker fetch() egress satisfies, and they serve SSR HTML with the data inline (__NEXT_DATA__ or JSON-LD), no XHR follow-up needed. Three suppliers moved from abandoned to worker-viable with no credentials, because the old verdicts predated the right probe.

Southwest and Princess validate an Apigee API key. The adapter hardcodes the last known good key and, on INVALID_API_KEY, retries once after scraping the SPA bundle for a fresh one. The gotcha that cost me a real debugging session: don't scrape greedily. The bundle carries several keys for different surfaces, and the first match is often valid for a surface other than the one you're calling, which still gets rejected.

Where the wall is

The deepest investigation characterized a modern Akamai BMP deployment end to end: eight Playwright configurations, two residential proxy vendors, and byte-level diffing of 491,810 sensor reads that came back byte-identical across an AT&T Mobility path and a Comcast residential path. The conclusion (2026-05-18) is that the gate is connection-layer proxy-indirection detection, down at L4. No amount of browser-fingerprint work touches that, and a Worker fetch() trips the same gate. The result is codified as ADR-0003 with explicit re-open triggers, so nobody burns a week re-testing Carnival-class suppliers without new evidence. Those suppliers run through Playwright in voygent-desktop, proxied behind the Lite MCP. I don't claim a live edge bypass there, because there isn't one.

Kasada (Southwest) is the one true browser-only case in scope: a client-side proof-of-work bundle, and Workers have no JS engine to run it. Beating it in Playwright took four stacked fixes: a real-Chrome UA override; the --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled C++ flag, because the Object.defineProperty JS mask is worse than no mask at all; a forced paint cycle, which in practice means calling page.screenshot() after goto; and a clean egress IP. It is the most expensive bypass in the whole catalog, which is exactly why it lives on the desktop side and not in a Worker.

What's next

TLS verdicts age. CDNs fingerprint specific Chrome builds, so curl-impersonate profiles go stale; as of 2026-05-29, wreq (formerly rnet) with a Chrome147 profile is fresher than curl_cffi's newest. The TLS-gate verdicts in the catalog predate the wreq rung of the ladder, so the next pass is re-probing those rows before trusting any of them.

record-replay-v2.title: Record/replay engineering
record-replay-v2.subtitle: How a public demo shows real data deterministically, with fabrication blocked in code instead of in the prompt.
record-replay-v2.body:
A public LLM demo has a credibility problem. If the model can write travel data into the page, it will eventually invent a flight. The first build of this demo did exactly that: the folio looked perfect, and some of what was on it didn't exist.

Prompting at the problem

My first response was the obvious one, telling the model more firmly not to make things up. That lowers the rate and proves nothing. A demo that fabricates once in fifty sessions is still a demo that fabricates, and I had no way to show a skeptical viewer that the data on screen was real. So I stopped trying to make the model trustworthy and took away its authority instead.

Capture once, replay byte for byte

For the five featured trips, a capture script runs the real production pipeline once: real searches, real candidate lists, and, the part that matters, the real promoted trip objects keyed by candidate id. The demo's replay layer intercepts the search tools and serves those captures. When the model picks a hotel, the server writes the captured object for that candidate id. The model authors only the id, never the data. An id with no fixture match is rejected. There is no code path by which model-invented data reaches the folio.

Live trips pass through

Ask for a destination outside the featured five and the session latches into live mode: every tool call passes through to the production Voygent MCP, the full tool catalog is exposed, and the folio renders exactly what read_trip returns. The featured trips are the rehearsed cut; live trips are the product, unsanitized.

Why the folio updates instantly here and slowly in production

Production Voygent talks to claude.ai through a connector, and a connector cannot push UI into the chat. So the production loop is a round trip: render the folio to R2, a human annotates the static page, the assistant reads the pending annotations, applies the batch, and re-renders. Published pages are pre-rendered R2 objects and stay stale until the next render. The demo owns its own front end, so it collapses that loop: the worker watches trip-mutating tool calls, re-projects the trip to fresh FolioBoardData, and pushes it over SSE; the client diffs and animates. Re-projection is deterministic compute, not an LLM call, so the live folio adds close to nothing to the bill.

The harness tests itself the same way

The same recording format drives the autoplay demo, and a headless smoke harness drives the full SSE pipeline against local or production: scripted board picks, sequencing assertions (no hotel board before a flight is picked), and an enrichment verdict at the end. Sessions survive Durable Object eviction by persisting conversation and replay state, so an idle reader doesn't orphan their trip. The rejected-id behavior and the client-data allowlist are unit-tested invariants, which is what I mean when I say the demo's honesty is an engineering property rather than a policy.

Future improvements

cost-engineering-v2.title: Cost engineering
cost-engineering-v2.subtitle: What an agent session actually costs, why caching changes the math, and why MCP economics favor the product.
cost-engineering-v2.body:
This demo runs a full agent loop on a public URL: Anthropic Messages API, streaming, the production tool catalog, anonymous traffic. That combination is a bill waiting to happen, so the cost had to be engineered before the demo could exist at all.

The problem with agent loops

An agent loop re-sends its whole history every turn. Twenty turns in, every new turn re-transmits nineteen turns of conversation, the entire tool catalog, and the seed prompt. Uncached, all of that re-bills as fresh input each time, so the cost of a session grows with the square of its length. That curve doesn't survive contact with a public URL.

Prompt caching does the heavy lifting

The fix is to place cache breakpoints on the three expensive prefixes: the tool catalog, the long static seed prompt, and a moving breakpoint on the final message, so the whole growing conversation is a cache hit on the next turn. Cache reads bill at roughly 0.1x fresh input; writes at about 1.25x. The Engineering tab reports the session's cache hit rate and a cost-weighted token figure (reads at 0.1x, writes at 1.25x). The cost-weighted number is the honest one to compare against a subscription window; the raw token sum reads five to ten times too pessimistic.

TODO(neil): a representative real session figure here (cents per built trip, typical hit rate) from the live stats would anchor this. The panel shows it live, but one concrete number in the prose would help.

A public endpoint needs more than caching

Caching controls the cost of a well-behaved session. A public endpoint also gets the other kind, so there are four independent guards. Per-conversation caps on turns and tool calls, enforced server-side. A global daily spend ledger in a reserved Durable Object, so the endpoint pauses itself at the cap instead of waiting for me to notice. An instant kill switch (a DEMO_DISABLED secret, no redeploy needed). And a destructive-tool denylist: the public catalog withholds deletes, client-facing publishes, and CRM writes, so the worst a hostile session can do is spend its own capped budget.

The MCP business case

The structural point sits underneath all of this: under the MCP model, the product's marginal inference cost is $0. The user's own Claude subscription pays for the tokens, and these sessions fit inside a plan's 5-hour window (the demo's plan table computes your session's exact share, cost-weighted). A standalone app has to meter API tokens, mark them up, and carry billing, abuse, and infrastructure liability that compounds with volume and model tier. An MCP product ships frontier-model reasoning at flat rate, and its costs don't scale with its users' usage.

What's next: cheaper models where they're good enough

The other lever is not paying frontier rates for non-frontier work. The demo has a provider seam with a gated DeepSeek driver for exactly this. To keep the claim honest: in production Voygent no free or local model runs today; the only server-side model calls are Claude-backed validate_trip and trip_checklist. A free-tier line on the demo's scoreboard, backed by Workers AI, is planned and I'm labeling it that way until it ships. The dev-time cousin is real, though: my llm-tools router sends bulk I/O (summaries, extraction) to a cheap model at about 1/125th of Opus prices.

production-system-v2.title: The system behind the demo
production-system-v2.subtitle: This demo fronts a production MCP product. These are the parts of that system that took real engineering.
production-system-v2.body:
This demo is a front end. Behind it is the production Voygent MCP: 119 tool registrations and about 30 supplier adapters across cruise, flight, hotel, package, car, and excursion, all running on Cloudflare Workers fetch(), with no browser and no VM for anything that probes worker-viable. One MCP server drives both Claude and ChatGPT in production: OAuth 2.1 with Dynamic Client Registration so claude.ai's connector flow authenticates without a pasted bearer token, per-user URL+token auth, and a tier-gated tool catalog locked per session (ADR-0004, no tools/list_changed). The adapters get their own page (the bot-defeat saga). This one is about the machinery around them, the parts production actually forced me to build.

The commission firewall

Advisors earn commission; clients must never see it. I made that separation a codified law rather than a convention, because conventions drift under refactoring. It is LAW 1 in LAWS.md, with a grep-verify. The client render path runs an explicit field allowlist, and the folio-board projector calls assertNoAdvisorKeys whenever the viewer role is client, so a leaked field fails loudly instead of rendering quietly. Commission and margin economics are served from separate routes behind bearer auth with no-store. This demo's advisor toggle is the inverse on purpose: demo boards are the advisor view, so commission shows up as a feature.

AI evaluating the AI

I wanted regression coverage for behavior as well as for code, and hand-testing an agent product doesn't scale past a handful of flows. So a persona/judge harness exercises the real product: Claude subagents role-play 13 advisor personas across 22 scenarios in four tiers, making real MCP calls. A judge model scores each transcript on four weighted dimensions (task completion 40%, UX 25%, data quality 20%, error handling 15%) against an EMA baseline, and alerts on drops bigger than 1.5 points. The loop closes itself: findings get filed as issues through the report_issue tool, a gate decides whether a finding warrants external review, a fix-prompt renderer produces a self-contained cold-start prompt (about 2 KB of failure-focused transcript), and a scenario synthesizer turns open issues into new regression scenarios. It lives in voygent-desktop and runs as a harness. I show it here as a static artifact and don't run it live, because a live run is real spend and real subagents.

Vendor onboarding as a pipeline

After enough hand-built adapters the shape was repeatable, so it became one command. /onboard probes a new supplier up the transport ladder (curl-impersonate, then Worker fetch, then Playwright), classifies the result through a consensus gate, scaffolds an adapter from a category-matched template (cruise-oidc, cruise-rest-csrf, cruise-rest-next-action, flight-jwt, hotel-aspnet-graphql, activity-cf-ja3-ssr, auth-nextauth-credentials), wires it into the router, Env, and tier catalog, generates vitest tests, and leaves a staged commit. The same skill has an --audit mode that re-runs a shipped adapter against captured baselines and files an issue when the supplier's site drifts, and audits can be scheduled. Adding a supplier is one command, and the fleet checks itself for rot.

Telemetry that can't hurt the hot path

Each tool call emits one Analytics Engine data point at the tier-gate chokepoint: surface, tool name, tier, user hash, error class, and session id in the blobs; duration and an ok flag in the doubles. The part I actually care about is defensive: it no-ops safely when the binding is absent, and there is an explicit unit test that it never throws even if the telemetry write itself throws. A measurement system that can take down the thing it measures is worse than no measurement system. This small stream is also the real per-tool latency source the demo's Inspector reuses.

Credentials I never see in the clear

Advisors bring their own supplier logins, and I didn't want to be able to read them. Each secret is envelope-encrypted under a per-user AES-256-GCM key in D1, and the vault tool returns only presence and metadata — never a stored value, not even to the advisor who set it. Every set, delete, and test writes an audit row; the scope is locked to travel-supplier portals; and a vendor's tools stay out of your catalog until its credentials exist. (ADR-0010.)

Nothing ships unverified

I gated production on itself. A prod deploy is refused unless a same-SHA staging smoke test passed within the hour and a seven-boundary security suite is green: cross-tenant isolation, the auth front door, call-time tier enforcement, the app-only data channel, render XSS, SSRF, and proxy/secret hygiene. Writing those tests turned up two real vulnerability classes, which is the whole point of writing them. Between deploys, a nightly QA digest and a token-gated ops dashboard keep an eye on it.

How this demo is built

The reel replays a real planning session through the same reducer the live app uses, so it is pixel-identical to a live run and costs nothing to play — and it cannot fabricate data, because replay returns fixtures and my authoring DSL refuses any pick that is not a real candidate id. The annotated callouts come from cueframe, a small tool I built for exactly this: I give it a URL and a plain-English workflow, it drives the page with Playwright, and it anchors each callout to a real DOM element rather than a fixed pixel, so the annotations don't slide off when the UI changes underneath them.

Future improvements

trip-integrity-v2.title: Trip integrity: the data is the product
trip-integrity-v2.subtitle: A weak model will ship a blank or broken proposal unless the server refuses to let it. Voygent owns data quality end to end.
trip-integrity-v2.body:
The validation panel in this demo's Engineering tab (the "validation N/N" stat and its passed, repaired, and failed checks) is the visible edge of a production stance: the trip data is the deliverable, so the server is what guarantees it is correct. It solves a different problem from record/replay. That feature keeps the public demo from showing invented data. This one keeps the live product from emitting a bad proposal in the first place.

The architecture I dropped

An earlier architecture split the work: one service wrote raw trip JSON and a second one reconciled it later. On paper that looked like a clean separation of concerns. In practice every data-quality flaw (duplicate booking shapes, a missing amount, a double-encoded HTML entity, a price that doesn't sum) surfaced far away from the code that produced it, so the fix kept landing in the reconciler when it belonged at the source. So the two halves became one: the product owns trip-data integrity end to end, and quality findings are bugs fixed on write, in a single place. That ownership is written down as a formal architecture decision so it can't quietly drift apart again.

Guards the model can't talk past

The strongest guards are the ones no prompt can argue with. The proposal renderer carries an empty-decisions guard: it refuses to publish a client proposal that has no choices in it, which is exactly the failure a rushed or cheap model produces. Behind it, a builder assembles the pickable options from the trip's state, and a completeness hint rides back to the model in the tool's response to point it at the gaps. On the write path, the server normalizes the data's shape and reconciles the pricing so the numbers add up before anything reaches a client.

Advisory versus blocking, on purpose

Not every warning should stop the world. Editing a trip returns non-blocking consistency signals ("this hotel's dates don't overlap the trip", "this leg has no price") that surface to the advisor without halting the build. The hard guards block a publish; the advisories simply inform a human. Over-blocking trains people to route around the guard, so keeping the two tiers separate is deliberate.

Self-heal: the repaired checks

Some problems are better fixed than flagged. A published proposal URL once resolved to /proposal/unknown because the trip id was missing from its metadata. The fix was quiet: the builder now stamps the trip id into the metadata at save time, and the render path repairs the link on the way out. Duplicate-booking shapes get normalized; double-encoded entities get decoded. Those runs show up as repaired in the panel, where the server caught a flaw and corrected it before it ever reached a client.

Checking my numbers against the public internet

Internal consistency isn't the whole job; the prices also have to survive contact with what a client can Google. A price sanity check compares advisor pricing against public OTA rates through SerpAPI (Google Flights and Google Hotels) and tags every block with its source and the date it was pulled, so a number renders as "$310/nt (SerpAPI / Google Hotels, 2026-04-18)" rather than a bare figure. SerpAPI is licensed and cheap (about $0.012 a search, 880 to 1792 ms, 23 OTA sources per hotel), which makes it safe to run live for anonymous demo traffic.

The same instinct, applied to money

The strictest integrity rule in the system is about money: advisors earn commission, and clients must never see it. The client render path runs a strict field allowlist that strips every advisor-only key, and the economics endpoints sit behind bearer auth and never cache. It is the first and hardest rule in the codebase, enforced automatically on every build; the longer story is on the system page.

Future improvements

The piece I want next is a background integrity sweeper: a scheduled pass over stored trips that flags what the live guards would catch (stale prices, dangling bookings) and proposes a fix for review instead of applying it on its own. It follows the same propose-don't-dispose pattern described on the subagents page, and it is on the roadmap rather than shipped today.

data-stores-v2.title: KV, D1, and rewiring a SQL brain
data-stores-v2.subtitle: Four storage primitives, one hybrid model, and the unlearning a career relational DBA has to do at the edge.
data-stores-v2.body:
I come from a relational world, and years of it train a reflex: normalize, index, join. Voygent runs on Cloudflare's edge, where "the database" is four primitives with sharply different shapes, and the reflex had to be retrained. The need was concrete. My early trip-planning attempts were prompting only, and the first thing they exposed was that I had no precise, persistent record of the plan, nothing I could retrieve, edit, and render from (that story starts on the context economics page). Once trip state became a real object, the question became where it should live.

The instinct I had to drop

My instinct said one relational store for everything: trips as rows, bookings as child tables, joins at read time. The edge fights that. Most reads here are "give me this one trip, whole," and an extra round trip at the edge costs more than the duplicated bytes ever will. Storage is cheap, and the join is the expensive part. So each kind of state goes to the primitive whose grain fits it, and no single store is asked to do all four jobs.

The four primitives

Workers KV is a global, eventually consistent key-to-value store: O(1) get and put by key, list by key prefix, no queries, no joins, and roughly 60 seconds of global propagation. Voygent keeps each trip blob here under a caller-prefixed key. D1 is SQLite at the edge: real SQL, transactions, indexes, FTS5 full-text search. It serves as the catalog, the queryable spine ("list this advisor's trips", "search trip content") that KV cannot express. R2 is object storage for binaries (rendered folio HTML, images, documents), served by path with no egress fees. And Durable Objects are single-writer, strongly consistent compute-plus-storage cells: this demo's per-session state (conversation, replay snapshot, the daily budget ledger) lives in one, because that is exactly the workload KV's eventual consistency can't safely hold.

The hybrid model

A trip is written twice, on purpose: as a KV blob (cheap, global, read-heavy) and as a D1 index row, so listing and searching stay single indexed queries. R2 holds what the client downloads. The DO holds the live session that must be consistent. Each store does the one thing it is shaped for.

What a SQL brain has to relearn

Key design is the schema. In KV there is no WHERE, only the key and its prefix, so you design the key so that every read you need is a get or a prefix list. Nothing else exists.

Joins are gone, so you denormalize on purpose: the fields a read needs get duplicated into the blob, so the read never has to assemble them from three places.

Eventual consistency is the default, and you plan for it. A KV write may not be globally visible for about a minute, so anything that needs read-your-writes (a counter, a lock, a budget ledger) belongs in a DO or in D1.

A list is an ordered prefix scan. Prefix scans paginate in key order, so sort order gets encoded into the key itself. This demo zero-pads its message keys (msg:00000) so a list comes back in conversation order: an ORDER BY, spelled as a key format.

Values have hard caps, and the caps will find you. A DO storage value tops out at 128 KiB, and a real tool-result bundle can exceed it. The session store learned this the hard way: the persisted copy elides its largest payloads to fit under the cap, while the in-memory copy stays whole.

And D1 is still there when a read genuinely earns an index: full-text search, ad-hoc filters, aggregates. The relational reflexes still have their place; they are just scoped now. You keep SQL where SQL earns its keep, and you stop paying join cost for reads that a well-designed key answers for free.

Future improvements

The storage split itself is settled. The open work here is operational: wider full-text coverage in D1, lifecycle rules for the R2 objects, and better migration tooling. Those are on the list and not yet built.

sources: the trip blob in Workers KV under a caller-prefixed key, the D1 catalog index, R2 for downloadable folios, the per-session Durable Object, and the 128 KiB value cap that shapes what gets persisted.

llm-options-v2.title: Choosing the model, and why the demo is LLM-agnostic
llm-options-v2.subtitle: Frontier, cheap, and local models behind one provider interface. The driving model is a configuration choice.
llm-options-v2.body:
Every agent product has to answer the question of which model drives it, and the honest answer changes every few months as prices and capabilities move. I didn't want that answer welded into the architecture. So everything the agent in this demo does (the tool catalog, the trip state, the record/replay honesty layer) sits behind a single provider interface, and the driving LLM is a configuration choice.

The seam

One TypeScript interface, LLMProvider.stream(messages, tools, opts), yields a normalized event stream: text deltas, tool calls, token usage. Anthropic's Claude is one implementation. A DeepSeekProvider over the OpenAI-compatible API is another. A minimal OllamaProvider for local models is a third. The agent loop consumes the normalized events and never learns which vendor produced them. Adding a provider is one interface implementation plus a pricing row.

To be precise about what ships where, because this is easy to overclaim: the seam and these drivers are demo code, in this repo. DeepSeek executes only when both an API key and a DEMO_DEEPSEEK_ENABLED flag are set, so it can ship dark and flip on deliberately. The production Voygent MCP's relationship to models is different and simpler: the same MCP server serves both claude.ai and ChatGPT as hosts in production, and its only server-side model calls are Claude-backed validate_trip and trip_checklist. No free or local model runs in the production Worker today.

Normalizing vendors is where the work was

The interface is small; the differences hide in the streams. DeepSeek only reports token usage on a streamed response if you ask for it (stream_options: {include_usage: true}), and a paid provider returning no usage is treated as an error rather than a silent $0, because the budget ledger depends on those numbers. Caching is provider-specific: Claude wants explicit cache_control breakpoints, DeepSeek does automatic prefix caching with no write concept at all, so the cache logic stays inside each driver instead of leaking into the loop. OpenAI-style streams deliver tool calls fragmented by index and need reassembly, and Ollama doesn't send call ids, so the driver synthesizes them. None of this is hard; all of it is exactly the kind of vendor detail the seam exists to contain.

Frontier, cheap, local

Claude is the default for the discovery phase: strongest reasoning and tool-use reliability, and Anthropic's prompt-cache breakpoints make a long agent loop affordable (cache reads bill at roughly 0.1x fresh input). DeepSeek is the cheap seat: very low per-token cost, automatic prefix caching, and good enough for the recipe-driven enrichment phase where the reasoning bar is lower; the "optimize for cost" preset routes there. Ollama is a model on your own machine: zero per-token cost, full data residency, offline-capable. In this demo it shows up grayed out, and the gray is honest: this UI is served from a Cloudflare edge Worker, which cannot reach a model listening on your localhost. The provider exists in code and lights up in a local-dev deployment where OLLAMA_BASE_URL is reachable.

Routing by phase

The Tweaks panel exposes three presets: speed favors the fastest small model, cost routes to the cheapest enabled provider, capability puts the strongest model on the reasoning-heavy phase. The interesting one is splitting a single trip across vendors, frontier discovery and cheap enrichment, which the seam makes a per-turn choice. The phase machine is what makes that safe: when the server holds the plan, the cheap model only ever has to do the one small step in front of it.

Honesty survives the swap

For the featured trips, the replay layer intercepts tool results, not the model, so swapping providers cannot open a fabrication path. A weaker model that picks a nonexistent option id gets rejected the same way a strong one would. The model-agnostic seam and the fabrication guard are orthogonal, by design.

What's next

Two things, both labeled as plans. A free or near-free model tier on the demo's scoreboard, built on Workers AI, so the cost column can show a $0.00 line; it is planned, not shipped. And routing production subtasks the same way the demo routes phases; the dev-time evidence that this pays is my llm-tools router, which sends bulk I/O to a cheap model at about 1/125th of Opus prices for summaries.

phase-machine-v2.title: Keeping the model on track
phase-machine-v2.subtitle: A server-side phase machine hands the model one small instruction at a time, which is what lets a cheaper model do the job reliably.
phase-machine-v2.body:
An open-ended agent loop asks a lot of a model: hold a twenty-turn plan in its head, decide what's next at every step, and never drift. A frontier model mostly manages it. A cheaper model mostly doesn't, and it fails in three specific ways I kept seeing. It stops early, declaring a trip done before enrichment. It presents instead of acting, asking "shall I add restaurants?" instead of calling the tool. And it narrates from memory, naming a plausible-sounding restaurant no tool ever returned. Each individual step is well within the small model's ability. The failures are discipline failures across a long sequence.

The open loop, and why I dropped it

The first version of this demo ran the obvious architecture: seed prompt, tool catalog, and trust the model to carry the build. With a frontier model driving, it mostly worked. With Haiku driving, it routinely stalled before enrichment, and no amount of prompt tightening made the stall rate zero, because the prompt was asking for twenty turns of sustained discipline rather than twenty small decisions. Production Voygent had already hit the same wall from a different angle: its trip builds run as a server-managed checklist (manage_trip_goal derives a goal, advance returns exactly one next action) precisely because letting the model batch many searches into one turn times out. The lesson from both: the sequencing doesn't belong in the model.

Move the sequencing into the server

The phase machine takes the build off the model's shoulders. A pure, unit-tested reducer (worker/agent/phases.ts) owns a small state machine, INTAKE → FLIGHT_PICK → HOTEL_SEARCH → HOTEL_PICK → ENRICH_EXCURSIONS → APPLY_PICKS → ENRICH_DINING → SUMMARY, and the worker, not the model, decides what happens next. Before each turn the model is handed one small directive: the current phase's instruction, and nothing else.

Advance by observation, never by trust

The machine only moves forward when it observes the right tool actually succeed. advancePhase(phase, toolName, input, result) watches the real tool-result stream: a successful flight_search moves INTAKE → FLIGHT_PICK, a successful promote_hotels_to_lodging moves HOTEL_PICK → ENRICH_EXCURSIONS. A failed or unrelated call doesn't advance anything. The model cannot talk its way forward; it has to do the thing.

Stalls get re-prompted, with a floor

When the model ends its turn without a tool call, the classic "I'll stop here," a capped auto-continuation re-issues the current phase's directive and keeps going, so the build can't quietly wedge half-finished. After a few re-prompts the machine forces the SUMMARY step, so a trip always ends with a clean closing message instead of trailing off. In the board-pick phases it deliberately does the opposite: a stop there is the model correctly waiting for the user, so it doesn't auto-continue.

What it bought

The acceptance bar for this work: with Claude Haiku driving, 10 out of 10 scripted Dublin builds produced a complete folio, meaning three or more day-by-day days, at least one free and one paid activity, four or more dining picks, and zero fabricated names. Before the phase machine, Haiku routinely stalled before enrichment. Same model. The difference is who holds the plan. That also makes per-phase model routing safe (the provider seam): when the structure carries correctness, the reasoning-light phases can run on the cheapest capable model.

Shipping it without betting the demo

The whole machine sits behind a single flag (DEMO_PHASE_MACHINE). Flag off, behavior is byte-identical to the previous open-loop path; flag on, the worker drives. It shipped dormant, was canaried on production, and rolls back by deleting one secret, no redeploy. The "Workflow engine" trail in this demo's Engineering panel shows each phase the server advanced through as your trip is built.

Future improvements

The same discipline pointed at production is the interesting next step: the orchestration that lets Haiku finish a demo trip is the thing that would make cheaper host models viable for the production MCP. That's a direction, not a commitment.

subagents-v2.title: Subagents for the drudge work
subagents-v2.subtitle: An agent that reads the inbox and drafts every action, and touches nothing until a human says go.
subagents-v2.body:
A travel advisor's day is full of necessary tedium: triaging a flooded inbox, pulling promo codes out of supplier blasts, matching a booking confirmation to the right active trip. This is exactly the work an agent should absorb, and exactly the work where a wrong autonomous action does real damage. A deleted email or a message sent to the wrong client is not a bug report, it's a lost client. The design answer I settled on: the agent does all the reading and all the drafting, and holds no authority to act. It proposes; the human disposes.

The one that runs today: the offers inbox

This part is live against a real advisor mailbox, not a roadmap item. An IMAP IDLE watcher (a systemd service) reacts to mail as it arrives. A Haiku-4.5 classifier sorts each message into one of 13 categories (promo blast, booking confirmation, client-active, supplier doc, junk, and so on), and anything below 0.6 confidence is parked as UNCERTAIN rather than guessed at. A second pass pulls structured offers (code, type, dates) out of the promo blasts and posts them into Voygent's shared offers index, where they become searchable inventory for trip-building. A trip-linker matches operational mail to the advisor's live trips. And every morning at 06:00 a digest lands as the advisor's triage queue. The digest is deterministic, pure SQL to markdown with zero LLM calls, so the one document the advisor acts on every day cannot hallucinate. The running tally: about 3,700 messages ingested, 2,300 classified, for roughly $4.50 of model spend.

Propose, never dispose

I didn't want the safety to be a promise in a prompt, so it's structural. The watcher opens the mailbox read-only: IMAP EXAMINE, never SELECT for write, so any code path that calls STORE, MOVE, EXPUNGE, or APPEND is a bug by definition, not a feature waiting for a flag. DRY_RUN is the default and the only permitted value in this phase: every action the agent recommends is written to an actions table with executed_at left NULL, a log of proposed moves with nothing performed. The advisor works the digest and decides. The constraint hierarchy is written down and ordered: mailbox safety, then classification correctness, then feature completeness, then speed. When two goals collide, the human's data wins.

Why this shape

TODO(neil): if there were earlier iterations worth recording (a different classifier, an autonomy level considered and rejected, a near-miss that motivated EXAMINE-only), that story belongs here. The source notes only document the design as landed.

Coming soon: the rest of the fleet

The offers agent is the first instance of a pattern, and the pattern generalizes to the rest of the drudge work. Each of these is coming soon, and each gets built the same propose-don't-dispose way. Offers surfaced inside the build: today the agent files offers into the index, next it raises the relevant ones during planning ("three of your suppliers are running Greece promos this week") as suggestions the advisor accepts, never auto-applied. An adapter-audit watchdog: the onboarding pipeline already has an --audit mode that re-runs a shipped adapter against captured baselines; run on a schedule as a subagent, it files an issue when a supplier site drifts, catching the breakage before an advisor hits it live. And a trip-integrity sweeper: a background pass that flags the data-quality issues the live guards would catch (stale prices, dangling bookings) and proposes the fix for review.

The principle is the same one behind the phase machine: don't ask the model for judgment it shouldn't hold. An agent can read a thousand emails and draft every action, and still touch nothing until a human says go. Keeping the advisor in the loop is the architecture, not a limitation bolted onto it.
